contact.why: C4590, C4790, C5090 and C5490 (final checkride) are the Contact evaluations, flown by IP evaluators per BD 3-1/HATC.
The last sortie of the Contact category, C5490, stands as the final examination for the category.

contact.topic: No SOLO after 59 percent or less
contact.why: An SP graded 59 percent or less on the previous flight, of any category, may not fly SOLO and continues dual in the category where he was graded ALMOST GOOD or FAIL.
SOLO is not flown more than four calendar days after the last front-seat dual VFR flight and requires at least MIF "2" in normal landing.
Stalls, spins and spin prevention, unusual attitudes, ELP, straight-in, slow flight, no-flap patterns/landings and simulated lost wingman may not be flown SOLO.
The previous dual grade sheet must record whether the SP is fit for SOLO and which maneuvers he was graded at least code "2" on.
The last flight of a Training Section may not be a SOLO.
An SP is not scheduled for two consecutive SOLO flights.
SOLO flights must land at the latest 30 minutes before sunset.
While a student is SOLO in the flight area or the airport circuit, a dual aircraft of the same type must be inside the KALAMATA MTMA.
Up to the PRE-SOLO phase the SP flies at most one aircraft and one F/S sortie per day.
C4101 is not graded in general performance unless air sickness occurs, in which case it is graded FAIR (59 percent) with no FCJ.
Both sorties are flown the same day with the same aircraft.

contact.topic: First SOLO counted as one sortie
contact.why: The pre-SOLO evaluation and the first SOLO count as a single sortie for maximum daily employment; if the SOLO cannot be flown the evaluation is repeated.
A DEFICIENCY or FAIL on the first SOLO leads to a Proficiency Examination with the same profile, because the first SOLO counts as the last flight of the Section.
ELPs are performed daytime and under VMC only.
Phase II ground training includes a written examination in the Basic Maneuvers of the Contact category.
The blind control examination precedes the C4790 checkride with a 90 percent pass mark, repeated the next day on failure.
SRC-1 to SRC-11 define the Contact special requirements from AGSM to ELP with IDLE power.

instrument.why: The last sortie of the Instrument category, I4890, stands as the final examination for the category.
In Instrument sorties the IP keeps responsibility for clearing and for remaining inside the assigned area.
Sections I45XX and I46XX require at least one IFR navigation and one instrument approach at a strange airfield per SP.
Sections I45XX and I46XX may be flown to Italian airfields or Cyprus under the BD 3-1/HATC fuel, weather and over-water restrictions.
Night IFR navigation I4701 requires I4501 and I3601 flown in night conditions and must precede I4603.
A landing at a foreign airport is graded with performance code "2".
At least one IFR navigation is flown with two external fuel tanks; the requirement may also be met in VFR navigation.
Mid-category evaluation grading at least one instrument descent and one final approach, plus IMC emergency procedures orally.
Flown as an IFR navigation with an instrument approach at a strange airport, optionally with two EFTs.
For the Instrument category the Squadron follows the F/S flow chart so performance improves gradually before the air sorties.
Where a section calls for IMC stimuli the simulator must present IMC optical elements, with cloud base and visibility criteria on approach and landing.
Written examinations in Basic Instruments, Advanced Instruments and IFR Navigation are part of Phase II ground training.
SRI-1 is spatial disorientation avoidance and SRI-2 is time and magnetic compass turns.

formation.why: The last sortie of the Formation category, F4690, stands as the final examination for the category.
Flight time is distributed equally between the Leader and Wingman roles subject to fuel and time.
T/O, echelon turns, close trail and extended trail as Wingman, and Cross Turns, are prohibited on SOLO flights.
The F43XX SOLO may be flown at F4301 on the same or next day as the last dual, the second within four calendar days; the F45XX SOLO the same or next day.
2.000 ft AGL for dual formation maneuvers, 6.000 ft AGL for extended trail, above 5.000 ft AGL for SOLO practice.
3.000 ft AGL for F43XX, 1000-3000 ft AGL for F45XX and above 5.000 ft AGL for the tactical formation SOLO.
Interval T/O, as Leader or Wingman, need not be demonstrated by the IP.
At least six instrument approaches across the category, three as Leader and three as Wingman; Closed GCA may replace one.
Sections F43XX, F44XX and F45XX require a VOR/DME or TACAN approach with or without GCA in both roles.
The first SOLO of each section may be flown at F4301 and F4501 respectively, under BD 3-1/HATC restrictions.
Two-ship final evaluation covering general, Leader and Wingman profiles plus oral emergency procedures with formation emphasis.
Formation SOLO flights must be escorted by an IP holding a category "B" or higher instructor licence.
Phase II includes written examinations in Formation and in Tactical Formation.
SRF-1 is practice in simulated lost wingman procedures.

vfr_navigation.why: The last sortie of the Navigation category, N4690, stands as the final examination for the category.
Low Level Navigation sorties may be flown only after C5201.
Flight time as lead or wingman is divided equally in every navigation sortie.
All Medium Level Navigation sorties are flown at or above the MSA of the legs.
The IP demonstrates one leg at 500 ft AGL in Sections N43XX and N45XX.
VFR navigation sorties must have at least 5 legs of 10 to 30 NM each.
Navigation sorties may land at a strange airfield if the SP returns the same day within BD 3-1/HATC minima.
The SP occupies the front seat in all navigation sorties.
The IP nominates the GPS legs at briefing; they may not exceed half the total legs and should be flown over sea.
An instrument approach is flown during RTB in at least one sortie of N41XX, N42XX and N43XX and, if possible, on N4690.
Final evaluation over low level navigation and two-ship formation, with oral emergency procedures and IP-nominated GPS legs.
The requirement for one navigation flown with two external fuel tanks may also be met in VFR navigation.
SRN-1 requires one leg of a navigation sortie to be flown at 500 ft AGL.
Phase II includes NA 190 written examination in VFR Navigation and LNAV 790 written examination in Low Level Navigation.

global_links.why: A flight counts as executed only if at least 75 percent of the syllabus requirements and more than 75 percent of the planned flight time were covered.
Table 3 turns a shortfall against the planned MIF code into DEFICIENCY or FAILURE: expected "2" graded "1" is DEFICIENCY, graded "0" or "E" is FAILURE.
Exceeding the planned code and later returning to the planned level is not regression.
Planned codes must be reached by the last sortie of the Section; the code achieved on that last sortie becomes the minimum for the first sortie of the next one.
Code "2" is defined as the minimum performance code for safe execution, because it is what allows the maneuver to be flown SOLO.
Whenever the IP must intervene to complete a maneuver, the SP is graded "0" or "D" (dangerous handling).
Specific criteria define codes "1" and "3", intermediate deviations give "2", smaller deviations give "4" and larger ones give "0" or "D".
General performance is graded on the percentage scale: 90-100 excellent, 75-89 very good, 60-74 good, 50-59 almost good (DEFICIENCY), 0-49 FAIL.
Each flight carries two grades: an absolute code per maneuver and a relative grade for general performance.
The minimum number in parentheses next to each maneuver must be practised by the end of the Section, otherwise an extra sortie or carry-over is granted.
Where no minimum number is given but the Section MIF is higher than the previous one, the maneuver is practised as much as needed to reach it.
A maneuver with no grading in the current Section is graded against the criteria of the Section actually being flown, provided it was analysed and briefed.
The SP must have met the performance criteria by the end of the Training Phase.

global_links.topic: The last sortie of a Section
global_links.why: The last sortie of each Section is decisive because the Section performance levels must be reached by then.

global_links.topic: Failure on the last sortie of a Section
global_links.why: Missing the planned codes on the last sortie of a Section sends the SP to a Proficiency Examination with a Squadron evaluator; a second shortfall applies PD 29/2020.
At evaluations and final examinations the SP must reach the codes printed in the MIF tables; otherwise general performance is DEFICIENCY or FAIL and PD 29/2020 applies.
A grade of 0-59 percent on an evaluation or final examination flight is itself a referral criterion for flying aptitude review.
In Progress Checks and Proficiency Examinations the SP must reach the codes of his last flight before the check.

global_links.topic: Progress Check by the Ops Officer
global_links.why: First rung of the ladder: 60 percent or above continues training with another IP, 0-59 percent moves to the Squadron Commander.

global_links.topic: Progress Check by the Squadron Commander
global_links.why: Second rung: 60 percent or above continues with another IP, 0-59 percent refers the SP to the Flying Ability Board.
The Ops Officer may judge once per phase and the Squadron Commander once, or twice if the previous Ops Officer check was below 60 percent.
KEPE is a short-term progress supervision program applied to students showing reduced performance.
Any sortie at 59 percent or less, two consecutive flights at 63 percent or less, two consecutive air-sickness events, or ground exam failures put the SP into KEPE.
Maximum entries per phase: twice for ground examination failures, twice for the Adaptation category, once per other air or F/S category.
Measures include one sortie per day, fewer instructors, additional ground training and non-graded F/S repetition flights.
Exit goals may be a specific code on given maneuvers, a specific general grade, success in a questionnaire or in consecutive oral examinations.
If progress is not as planned the IP must propose KEPE, propose a day off flying, or grade the flight 0-59 percent for unacceptable progress.
Repetitions, non-executed flights, reassignment and habituation flights are not graded in general performance, but the grade sheet is filled in with codes and detailed remarks.
Air and ground evaluations are made against the performance criteria (STANDARDS) set by the training order in force for each phase.
No SP finishes the phase with less than 77,0 dual and 6,0 SOLO flight hours; all SOLO sorties are mandatory.
Every maneuver not practised in the F/S is demonstrated in the air at least once by the IP before the SP is asked to fly it.
Codes for maneuvers that need optical stimuli are not taken into account when the exercise is flown in the UTD.
No SP begins a Training Section or Exercise without having attended and been successfully evaluated on its ground-training objects.
Special requirements are annotated separately in the grade sheet with their corresponding performance levels.
Performance criteria split into General and Specific; the IP grades the General ones against SP experience and the current Training Section.
An SP may be within the published limits and still fail for instability, imprecision or hesitation.
Momentary excursions beyond PLUS/MINUS limits are acceptable only if corrected at once, without IP prompting or intervention.
Knowledge and procedures must follow the standardization of the Manuals and Squadron instructions.

global_links.topic: Demo-only maneuvers and missing specific criteria
global_links.why: Maneuvers only demonstrated are cited in the grade-sheet remarks; where no specific criteria exist, general and Basic A/C Control criteria apply.
Maneuvers are graded by day in VMC or IMC unless the criteria say otherwise, and VMC criteria must be met together with spatial awareness.
